questions.prompt: The scalar system is \(\dot x = -x^3 + u\). It rests at \(x = 2\), which needs \(u = 8\). The linearized \(A = \partial f/\partial x\) there is
questions.explanation: \(\partial f/\partial x = -3x^2\). At \(x = 2\) that is \(-12\), so \(A = -12\). The value \(-3x = -6\) drops one factor of \(x\). The equilibrium input 8 is \(u_e\), not the Jacobian.

questions.figure_alt: A row of two partial derivatives.

questions.prompt: For the same \(\dot x = -x^3 + u\), the input Jacobian \(B = \partial f/\partial u\) is
questions.explanation: The input enters as \(+u\), so \(B = 1\) at every state. Using \(A = -12\) as if it were \(B\) mixes the two partial derivatives. Using \(u_e = 8\) reports the equilibrium input instead of the slope in \(u\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>jacobian entries</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">df/dx   df/du</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A row of two partial derivatives.

questions.prompt: A tank obeys \(\dot h = -2\sqrt{h} + q\). It rests at \(h = 9\). The linearized coefficient of \(\delta h\) is
questions.explanation: The derivative of \(-2 h^{1/2}\) is \(-h^{-1/2} = -1/3\) at \(h = 9\), so \(A = -0.333333\). The outflow \(-2\sqrt{9} = -6\) is the equilibrium flow, not the slope. Half of that slope, \(-1/6\), comes from differentiating \(\sqrt{h}\) and forgetting the constant 2, or from differentiating and then dividing an extra time.

questions.prompt: A pendulum linearizes, near the bottom, to \(\ddot\theta + (g/L)\theta = 0\) with \(g/L = 10\). The natural frequency of that small motion is
questions.explanation: The standard form is \(\ddot\theta + \omega_n^2\theta = 0\), so \(\omega_n = \sqrt{g/L} = \sqrt{10} = 3.16228\). The ratio \(g/L = 10\) is \(\omega_n^2\), not \(\omega_n\). Half of 10 is not the square root.

questions.prompt: Near the origin, \(\dot x_1 = x_2\) and \(\dot x_2 = -2 x_1 + 0.5 x_2^2 + u\). The determinant of the Jacobian \(A\) is
questions.explanation: The quadratic term \(0.5 x_2^2\) has zero derivative at the origin, so \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Its determinant is \(2\), stored as 2. The trace is 0, which is not the determinant. The entry \(-2\) is one corner of \(A\), not \(\det A\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 168" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>mass, spring, and damper</title><rect x="16" y="36" width="14" height="100" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><line x1="30" y1="70" x2="48" y2="70"/><polyline points="48,70 56,58 66,82 76,58 86,82 96,58 106,82 116,70 140,70"/><text x="90" y="50" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">k</text><line x1="30" y1="112" x2="78" y2="112"/><rect x="78" y="100" width="28" height="24"/><line x1="106" y1="112" x2="140" y2="112"/><text x="92" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">b</text><rect x="140" y="48" width="64" height="80"/><text x="172" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">m</text><line x1="204" y1="88" x2="250" y2="88"/><polygon points="250,88 243.6,90.7 243.6,85.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="258" y="92" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">F</text><line x1="30" y1="148" x2="230" y2="148"/></svg>

questions.prompt: Return to \(\dot x = -x^3 + u\), now at the equilibrium \(x = 1.5\). The state Jacobian \(A\) is
questions.explanation: \(A = -3x^2 = -3\cdot 2.25 = -6.75\). The value at \(x = 2\), which is \(-12\), belongs to a different equilibrium. The equilibrium input \(u = x^3 = 3.375\) is not \(A\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>jacobian entries</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">df/dx   df/du</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A row of two partial derivatives.

questions.prompt: The system \(\dot x = x(1-x) + u\) rests at \(x = 3\). The linearized \(A\) is
questions.explanation: \(f = x - x^2 + u\), so \(A = 1 - 2x = 1 - 6 = -5\). The factor \(1 - x = -2\) forgets the product rule and is not the derivative of \(x - x^2\). The equilibrium input, which is 6, is \(u_e\), not \(A\).

questions.figure_alt: A complex pair of pole marks in the left half-plane.

options: building one linear model and using it at every operating point
cancelling every nonlinearity exactly, with no model error
ignoring equilibria and controlling the full nonlinear vector field
building a family of Jacobians along an operating curve and switching the controller as the state moves
questions.explanation: Each equilibrium has its own Jacobian, so a scheduled controller carries several local models and interpolates among them. One model is ordinary linear control. Exact cancellation of the nonlinearity is feedback linearization, a different construction. The equilibria are exactly where each local model is built.

questions.prompt: The scalar system \(\dot x = x - x^3\) has an equilibrium at \(x = 1\). The Jacobian there is
questions.explanation: \(A = 1 - 3x^2\). At \(x = 1\), \(A = -2\). At the origin the same formula gives \(+1\), which is the unstable equilibrium, not this one. The value \(-3x = -3\) drops a factor of \(x\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a stable real pole of the linearization</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="92" y2="90"/><line x1="120" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="85" x2="111" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="95" x2="111" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: One pole mark on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that builds the local matrices at an equilibrium.
questions.explanation: The resting condition comes first. A derivative at a point that is not an equilibrium is a different expansion. The state derivative is the matrix \(A\) and the input derivative is the matrix \(B\). Both are numbers only after they are evaluated at the resting pair. Swapping the two derivatives assigns the input slope to the state matrix.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>State and input partials</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">A   B</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two blocks, one for the state partial and one for the input partial.
steps: Confirm the chosen state and input make the rate zero.
Differentiate the rate with respect to the state.
Differentiate the rate with respect to the input.
Evaluate both derivatives at that equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Which eigenvalue patterns say the linear model at the equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable?
options: Every eigenvalue has a negative real part.
One eigenvalue is positive and the others are negative.
An eigenvalue has real part zero.
A repeated eigenvalue is fine when every real part is still negative.
questions.explanation: Local asymptotic stability of the linear model follows from every real part being negative, whether or not an eigenvalue is repeated. One positive real part makes the equilibrium unstable. A zero real part makes this test inconclusive. The test reads the eigenvalues of the Jacobian. It does not ask the nonlinear system to have only one equilibrium.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>A conjugate pair in the left half-plane</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="63" x2="111" y2="73" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="73" x2="111" y2="63" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="107" x2="111" y2="117" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="117" x2="111" y2="107" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A complex conjugate pair in the left half-plane.

questions.prompt: A note claims local asymptotic stability from the Jacobian. Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: A zero real part makes the linearization test inconclusive. It does not prove local asymptotic stability. The equilibrium check is the right first step, and a positive real part would indeed mean the linear model is unstable. The eigenvalues can be read from the Jacobian only after that Jacobian is evaluated at the equilibrium.

questions.figure_alt: Two marks, one in the left half-plane and one on the vertical axis.
steps: The chosen pair is an equilibrium, so the rate is zero there.
A zero eigenvalue still lets the linearization test conclude local asymptotic stability.
A positive real part would have made the equilibrium unstable.
reasons: A zero real part makes the linearization test inconclusive.
A zero eigenvalue proves stability on its own.
The equilibrium check is the false step.
